query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Subjecting equal‐atomic NbMoTaW to severe plastic deformation via high‐pressure torsion (HPT) will refine its coarse BCC grains into a uniform submicron-grained structure. This grain refinement is expected to enhance room-temperature ductility by increasing the grain boundary density (which facilitates dislocation nucleation and absorption) without altering the inherent BCC lattice that imparts its high-temperature mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW produced by conventional methods (e.g., arc melting or SLM) having a single-phase BCC structure with relatively coarse grain size and intrinsically poor room-temperature ductility, yet excellent strength at 1600 °C and irradiation resistance as predicted by first-principles calculations.
generation.intervention: Apply high-pressure torsion (HPT) processing to the fully dense NbMoTaW to induce severe plastic deformation and achieve a submicron-grained BCC structure.
generation.conditions: Process samples in an inert atmosphere using HPT at pressures around 2.5 GPa for approximately 15 revolutions. Test mechanical properties at room temperature, under high-temperature conditions (1600 °C), and after subjecting samples to irradiation doses comparable to those considered in baseline studies.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size refinement from coarse (tens of microns) to submicron levels increases the density of grain boundaries, which serve as effective sites for dislocation emission and defect recombination.
generation.mechanism: The severe plastic deformation induced by HPT refines the grain structure, thereby transforming the brittle behavior at room temperature into a more ductile response as grain boundaries aid in dislocation mobility and local plasticity. At high temperatures, the intrinsic strength of the BCC lattice is maintained, while the increased grain boundary area also provides enhanced sinks for irradiation-induced defects, preserving the alloy's radiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline, the HPT-processed alloy is predicted to exhibit a significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., a markedly higher fracture strain), while maintaining similar high yield and fracture strengths at 1600 °C and retaining its irradiation resistance. The refined microstructure should allow more homogeneous plastic deformation at ambient conditions without detrimental phase changes.
generation.baseline: Untreated NbMoTaW, which is a single-phase BCC refractory HEA with excellent high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation resistance (as predicted by first-principles), yet displays very poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected provided that (1) the HPT processing yields a uniform, fully dense submicron-grained microstructure without introducing deleterious contamination or unwanted secondary phases; (2) the refined structure remains stable during high-temperature exposure; and (3) processing conditions do not induce excessive residual stresses that could offset ductility improvements.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how the ultra-fine grain structure will respond under extreme high-temperature conditions or prolonged irradiation; there is also potential risk that HPT-induced residual stresses or contamination could negatively impact either the high-temperature mechanical properties or the irradiation resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW samples: one set as a control using standard processing and another subjected to HPT (e.g., 2.5 GPa for 15 revolutions) under an inert atmosphere. Characterize the microstructure using SEM and TEM to evaluate grain size and phase purity. Subsequently, perform mechanical tests at room temperature to measure ductility (tensile/compressive strain-to-failure), conduct high-temperature mechanical tests at 1600 °C, and expose both sets to controlled irradiation (e.g., ion irradiation simulating fusion-relevant doses). Compare the properties of the HPT-processed samples to the control.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase characterization (via SEM/TEM/XRD)
High-temperature yield strength and fracture strength (at 1600 °C)
Irradiation-induced defect density and microstructural stability (via TEM, APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HPT-processed NbMoTaW does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., less than a 50% increase in ductility or strain-to-failure) relative to the untreated baseline, or if its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance is measurably degraded (such as lowered yield strength at 1600 °C or increased defect clustering post-irradiation), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite processing challenges, and how do its microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance compare to traditional superalloys and arc-melted counterparts?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); parameters included hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, and a triple-pass remelting strategy (3x energy input) to achieve a linear energy density of 2.83 J/mm.
